title: What is the principle of least privilege: give users and services the MINIMUM permissions they need to do their job, not more?
topicTitle: Web Vulnerabilities: SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF
keyPoints: Least privilege means every user, service, and credential gets only the minimum permissions needed for its function.
It limits blast radius: a compromised identity can only do the small set of things it was explicitly allowed.
It applies at every layer: application roles, database grants, cloud IAM policies, file permissions, and network access.
Just-in-time elevation grants extra rights only for the minutes needed, then automatically revokes them.
Common anti-patterns: wildcard permissions, shared admin accounts, and temporary grants that never get removed.
In banking, least privilege is often a regulatory requirement, not just good engineering practice.

s1_definition.oneliner: Grant the minimum permission needed so a compromise can do minimum damage.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Principle of least privilege (PoLP)** – every user, service, process, and credential should be granted only the minimum permissions required to perform its function, and nothing more.
- **Blast radius** – limits the damage of mistakes, bugs, and compromised accounts by confining what a breached identity can do.
- **Multi-layer** – applies at application roles, database grants, cloud IAM policies, file permissions, and network access.
- **Just-in-time elevation** – grant extra rights only for the duration needed, then revoke automatically.
- **Separation of duties** – no single identity can both initiate and approve a sensitive action.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a teller's key opens only the teller drawer, not the vault, and a cleaner's pass opens only the lobby, not the server room. Nobody carries a master key just in case. If a teller's key is stolen, the thief reaches only the teller drawer, not the whole bank. Least privilege is the bank handing each person and each machine exactly the keys their job needs and no more, so one lost key cannot open everything.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Least Privilege Layers:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Application Layer                     │
  │   Reporting: SCOPE_account:read only │
  │   Transfer:  SCOPE_transfer:write    │
  │   Admin:     SCOPE_admin (JIT only)  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Database Layer                        │
  │   reporting_user: SELECT only        │
  │   transfer_user: SELECT, INSERT, UPD │
  │   No user has DROP or superuser      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Cloud IAM Layer                       │
  │   Specific actions on specific ARNs  │
  │   No wildcard * permissions          │
  │   Roles assumed temporarily          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ OS / Network Layer                    │
  │   Non-root service accounts          │
  │   Minimal open ports                 │
  │   Network segmentation               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The principle of least privilege says that every user, service, process, and credential should be granted only the minimum permissions needed to do its job, and nothing more. Its purpose is to limit the blast radius: if an identity is compromised or makes a mistake, it can only affect the small set of things it was explicitly allowed to touch. It applies at every layer: application roles and scopes, database grants, cloud IAM policies, file permissions, and network access.

In the National Bank of India project, this is applied concretely. The reporting service only needs to read balances for dashboards, so it gets a read-only scope and nothing else; even if it is compromised, it cannot move money because it never held write access. At the database layer the application user is granted only the statements it needs, and in the cloud, specific actions are granted on specific resources rather than wildcard permissions.

For sensitive actions, least privilege is paired with just-in-time, time-bounded elevation. A read-only service reads successfully but is blocked by deny-by-default when it tries to write, and an admin receives a ten-minute elevation that automatically expires afterward, so a stolen admin session outside that window cannot do the privileged action.

The nuances to stress are separation of duties so no single identity can both initiate and approve a sensitive transfer, avoiding the classic anti-patterns of wildcard permissions, shared admin accounts, and temporary grants that never get removed, and running regular access reviews to catch privilege creep. In a bank this is not just good hygiene: it is frequently a regulatory requirement.

Remember one sentence: grant the minimum permission needed for the job so a single compromise cannot open the vault.
